# Flow Processes (Open Systems) {#sec-ch4}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Demonstrate key concepts related to open systems (e.g. **steady-state** vs.
  **transient**, **mass flow rate**, and **flow work**).
- Apply **mass** and **energy** balances to open systems.
- Analyse different open systems such as **nozzles**, **diffusers**,
  **turbines**, **compressors** and **boilers**.
:::

## Introduction

In previous chapters, we developed the energy equation for a **closed system**
(i.e. a control mass), which exchanges only *energy* with its surroundings.
Many applications in thermodynamics, however, are regarded as open systems. An
**open system** (also called a **control volume**, or simply **CV**) is a
system that freely exchanges both **energy** and **mass** with its
surroundings.

![A jet engine and a dam spillway are open systems: the red dashed line marks a control volume that the fluid flows through. Heat, work *and mass* cross the boundary of an open system.](figures/img/ch4-open-systems.png){width=92%}

### Steady-state vs. transient conditions

Many engineering systems (e.g. turbines, compressors, nozzles, boilers and
condensers) can be idealised as being **steady state**, meaning that the
conditions of the system (e.g. its total mass and energy) **do NOT vary with
time**.

![Fluid flows in and out of the control volume (dashed), but at steady state the amount of mass and energy inside it stays the same.](figures/img/ch4-steady-cv.png){width=36%}

::: {.key}
$$
\text{Steady-state condition:}\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}E_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}m_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0
$$
$$
\text{Transient condition:}\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}(\;)_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} \neq 0
$$
:::

## Conservation of mass (continuity equation)

The **conservation of mass** principle for a control volume states that:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\text{rate of mass change}\\ \text{within the control volume}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\text{rate of mass}\\ \text{flux at inlet}\end{bmatrix}
-
\begin{bmatrix}\text{rate of mass}\\ \text{flux at exit}\end{bmatrix}
$$

![Mass enters the control volume at inlet $i$ at the rate $\dot{m}_i$ and leaves at exit $e$ at the rate $\dot{m}_e$.](figures/img/ch4-mass-balance-cv.png){width=36%}

::: {.key}
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}m_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{m}_i - \dot{m}_e
$$
where $\dot{m}_i$ and $\dot{m}_e$ are the **mass flow rates** at the inlet and
the exit, in kg/s.
:::

### Mass flow rate

We can obtain a mathematical expression for the mass flow rate $\dot{m}$
entering or exiting a control volume in terms of fluid local properties.

![In a time $\mathrm{d}t$, a slice of fluid of mass $\mathrm{d}m$, cross-sectional area $A$ and thickness $\mathrm{d}x$ (volume $\mathrm{d}V$) flows into the control volume.](figures/img/ch4-mass-flow-element.png){width=44%}

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Mass of the slice: $\mathrm{d}m = \rho\,\mathrm{d}V = \rho A\,\mathrm{d}x$; the velocity is $C = \mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t$."}
The mass of the slice, and the velocity of the fluid, are
$$
\mathrm{d}m = \rho\,\mathrm{d}V = \rho A\,\mathrm{d}x,
\qquad
C = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\;\;\text{(velocity)}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Divide by $\mathrm{d}t$: $\dot{m} = \rho A\,\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t = \rho A C$."}
Dividing by $\mathrm{d}t$:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{m}
= \rho A \underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}}_{C}
= \rho A C
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="With $\rho = 1/v$: $\dot{m} = AC/v$."}
and since $\rho = 1/v$,
$$
\dot{m} = \frac{AC}{v}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\dot{m} = \rho A C = \frac{AC}{v}
$$ {#eq-ch4-mdot}
:::

::: {.example}
A gas is flowing into a 1-m-diameter pipe at a uniform velocity of 10 m/s. The
temperature is 27 °C and the pressure is 100 kPa. Determine the mass flow rate.
(Assume ideal gas with $R = 200~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**Step 1.** *To use $\dot{m} = AC/v$ you need the specific volume. Which
equation gives $v$ from $P$ and $T$? Remember to use kelvin.*

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="$Pv = RT$: $v = RT/P = 200 \times 300/(100\times10^3) = 0.6~\mathrm{m^3/kg}$."}
Ideal gas, with $T = 27 + 273 = 300$ K:
$$
Pv = RT
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
v = \frac{RT}{P}
  = \frac{200~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times 300~\mathrm{K}}{100\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}}
  = 0.6~\mathrm{m^3/kg}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Now the area of the pipe, and @eq-ch4-mdot.*

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="$\dot{m} = AC/v = (\pi/4)(1)^2 \times 10/0.6 = 100\pi/24 \approx 13.1$ kg/s."}
With $D = 1$ m and $C = 10$ m/s:
$$
\dot{m} = \frac{AC}{v}
= \frac{\tfrac{\pi}{4}\,(1~\mathrm{m})^{2} \times 10~\mathrm{m/s}}{0.6~\mathrm{m^3/kg}}
= \frac{100\pi}{24}~\mathrm{kg/s}
\approx \boxed{13.1~\mathrm{kg/s}}
$$
:::
:::

### Steady-state form of mass conservation

For a steady-state condition, the total amount of matter within the control
volume remains constant. In general, with several inlets and exits,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}m_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum \dot{m}_i - \sum \dot{m}_e
$$

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Steady state: $\mathrm{d}m_{cv}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$, so what flows in flows out."}
At steady state $\mathrm{d}m_{cv}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$, so
$$
\sum \dot{m}_i = \sum \dot{m}_e
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="10mm" hint="Only one inlet and one outlet: $\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e = \dot{m}$."}
With only **one inlet** and **one outlet**:
$$
\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e = \dot{m}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\text{Steady state:}\qquad \sum \dot{m}_i = \sum \dot{m}_e
\qquad\xrightarrow{\ \text{one inlet/outlet}\ }\qquad
\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e = \dot{m}
$$
:::

## Conservation of energy for a control volume

The conservation of energy applied to a control volume (an open system) states:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\text{rate of energy}\\ \text{change within the}\\ \text{control volume}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\text{net rate of energy}\\ \text{transfer by heat}\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}\text{net rate of energy}\\ \text{transfer by work}\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}\text{net rate of energy}\\ \text{transfer by mass fluxes}\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](figures/img/ch4-energy-cv.png){width=50%}

Each unit of mass crossing the boundary carries its own energy with it: internal,
kinetic and potential, $u + \tfrac{1}{2}C^{2} + gz$ per kg (CH2).

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Over a short time: $\mathrm{d}E_{cv} = \delta Q + \delta W$ + energy carried in by $\mathrm{d}m_i$ $-$ energy carried out by $\mathrm{d}m_e$."}
Over a short time interval, a mass $\mathrm{d}m_i$ enters and a mass
$\mathrm{d}m_e$ leaves:
$$
\mathrm{d}E_{cv} = \delta Q + \delta W
+ \underbrace{\mathrm{d}m_i\left(u_i + \tfrac{1}{2}C_i^{2} + g z_i\right)
- \mathrm{d}m_e\left(u_e + \tfrac{1}{2}C_e^{2} + g z_e\right)}_{\text{energy by mass fluxes}}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Divide by $\mathrm{d}t$ to get rates."}
Dividing by $\mathrm{d}t$ gives the rate form below.
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}E_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{Q} + \dot{W}
+ \dot{m}_i\left(u_i + \tfrac{1}{2}C_i^{2} + g z_i\right)
- \dot{m}_e\left(u_e + \tfrac{1}{2}C_e^{2} + g z_e\right)
$$
:::

### Flow work

Consider a fluid element entering the control volume. The flow immediately
upstream will force this fluid element to enter the control volume, and can be
regarded as an *imaginary piston*. In other words, **flow work** is the work
**done by the surroundings** *at the inlet* to push the fluid element into
the control volume. Likewise, work is **done by the system** *at the exit*
to push the fluid element out of the control volume into the surroundings.

![The fluid just upstream acts as an imaginary piston that pushes a fluid element (red) into the control volume; at the exit the fluid in the control volume pushes an element out.](figures/img/ch4-flow-work.png){width=80%}

The work of the imaginary piston is expansion/compression work,
$\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$ (CH2).

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Inlet: the element of mass $\mathrm{d}m_i$ is pushed in, so the volume outside shrinks: $\mathrm{d}V_i = -v_i\,\mathrm{d}m_i$, and $\delta W_i = -P_i\,\mathrm{d}V_i = P_i v_i\,\mathrm{d}m_i$."}
At the inlet, an element of mass $\mathrm{d}m_i$ is pushed in, so the volume on
the upstream side decreases by $\mathrm{d}V_i = -v_i\,\mathrm{d}m_i$:
$$
\delta W_i = -P_i\,\mathrm{d}V_i = P_i v_i\,\mathrm{d}m_i
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Divide by $\mathrm{d}t$: $\dot{W}_i = P_i v_i \dot{m}_i$."}
$$
\dot{W}_i = P_i v_i \frac{\mathrm{d}m_i}{\mathrm{d}t} = P_i v_i \dot{m}_i
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Exit: the element is pushed OUT, $\mathrm{d}V_e = v_e\,\mathrm{d}m_e$, so the work has the opposite sign: $\dot{W}_e = -P_e v_e \dot{m}_e$."}
At the exit the element is pushed *out* by the system,
$\mathrm{d}V_e = +v_e\,\mathrm{d}m_e$, so
$$
\dot{W}_e = -P_e v_e \dot{m}_e
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\dot{W}_f = \dot{W}_i + \dot{W}_e = \dot{m}_i P_i v_i - \dot{m}_e P_e v_e
\qquad\text{(flow work rate)}
$$
:::

It is convenient to separate the **total work rate $\dot{W}$** into *two
contributions*: (i) the **flow work rate** $\dot{W}_f$ associated with the mass
fluxes at inlets and outlets, and (ii) all other work rates, denoted by
$\dot{W}_{CV}$, due to interaction with external sources, such as those
associated with rotating shafts, displacement of the boundary, and electrical
work.

::: {.key}
$$
\dot{W} = \underbrace{\dot{W}_f}_{\text{flow work}}
+ \underbrace{\dot{W}_{CV}}_{\text{piston, shaft, electrical}}
$$
:::

![A control volume can exchange work through a moving boundary (piston) and a rotating shaft (paddle), as well as flow work at its inlet and outlet.](figures/img/ch4-work-types.png){width=38%}

### Final form of the energy equation for a control volume

Substituting the flow work rate $\dot{W}_f$ into the energy equation results in:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}E_{CV}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{Q}_{CV} + \dot{W}_{CV}
+ \underbrace{\dot{m}_i P_i v_i - \dot{m}_e P_e v_e}_{\text{flow work}}
+ \dot{m}_i\left(u_i + \tfrac{1}{2}C_i^{2} + g z_i\right)
- \dot{m}_e\left(u_e + \tfrac{1}{2}C_e^{2} + g z_e\right)
$$

Recall the **enthalpy** from CH3, a property that combines the internal energy
with the product $Pv$:

::: {.key}
$$
h = u + P v
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Steady state: $\mathrm{d}E_{cv}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$."}
**Steady state:**
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}E_{cv}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Group each flow-work term with the internal energy at the same port: $\dot{m}_i(P_iv_i + u_i) = \dot{m}_i h_i$, and the same at $e$."}
The flow work combines with the internal energy at each port into the enthalpy:
$$
\dot{m}_i\left(P_i v_i + u_i\right) = \dot{m}_i h_i,
\qquad
\dot{m}_e\left(P_e v_e + u_e\right) = \dot{m}_e h_e
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="One inlet/outlet: $\mathrm{d}m_{cv}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ so $\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e = \dot{m}$; take out $\dot{m}$ and move the heat and work to the left."}
**One inlet/outlet:** $\mathrm{d}m_{cv}/\mathrm{d}t = 0$, so
$\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e = \dot{m}$. Taking $\dot{m}$ out as a common factor and
rearranging gives the equation below.
:::

::: {.key}
**Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE):**
$$
\dot{Q}_{CV} + \dot{W}_{CV}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right)
+ g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-ch4-sfee}
:::

::: {.note}
The **Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE)** is the basic equation for studying
most *open systems* in thermodynamics.
:::

::: {.warning}
Do NOT confuse the *SFEE for open systems* with the *energy equation for closed
systems*.
:::

**Open systems (flow processes):**
$$
\dot{Q}_{CV} + \dot{W}_{CV}
= \dot{m}\left[\underbrace{\left(h_e - h_i\right)}_{\text{enthalpy}}
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
$$

**Closed systems (non-flow processes):**
$$
Q + W = \Delta E
= m\left[\underbrace{\left(u_2 - u_1\right)}_{\text{internal energy}}
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_2^{2} - C_1^{2}\right) + g\left(z_2 - z_1\right)\right]
$$

| | Open systems (flow processes) | Closed systems (non-flow processes) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Property in the equation | enthalpy, $h$ | internal energy, $u$ |
| Each term is | a **rate** of energy [J/s] | an **amount** (form) of energy [J] |
| Applies to | a **steady** state, $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ | an **unsteady** process, from state 1 to state 2 |

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Open system: fluid flows through from $i$ to $e$, and nothing inside changes with time.](figures/img/ch4-open-sketch.png){width=62%}

![Closed system: the same mass goes from state 1 to state 2.](figures/img/ch4-closed-sketch.png){width=80%}
:::

## Examples of steady-state flow processes

### Nozzles and diffusers

A **nozzle** is a flow passage in which the velocity of a gas or liquid
*increases* in the direction of flow. In a **diffuser**, the gas or liquid
velocity *decreases* in the direction of flow.

![](figures/img/ch4-nozzle-diffuser.png){width=58%}

| Nozzle | Diffuser |
|:--|:--|
| $A_e < A_i$ | $A_e > A_i$ |
| $C_e > C_i$ | $C_e < C_i$ |

SFEE equation:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
$$

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Nozzle/diffuser: $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$ (fast flow, little time for heat transfer), $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$ (no shaft), $z_e \approx z_i$."}
In a nozzle or a diffuser there is little heat transfer, $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$;
there is no shaft or moving boundary, $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$; and the change of
height is negligible, $g(z_e - z_i) \approx 0$. With $\dot{m} \neq 0$:
$$
\left(h_e - h_i\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) \approx 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Mass balance, one inlet/outlet: $\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e$, with $\dot{m} = \rho A C$."}
And from conservation of mass, with $\dot{m} = \rho A C$:
$$
\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\rho_i A_i C_i = \rho_e A_e C_e
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\text{Nozzles and diffusers:}\qquad
\left(h_e - h_i\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) \approx 0,
\qquad
\rho_i A_i C_i = \rho_e A_e C_e
$$
:::

::: {.example}
Gas at 200 K enters an insulated nozzle with a velocity of 10 m/s. It leaves
the nozzle at a velocity of 600 m/s. Determine the final temperature. (Assume
ideal gas with $c_p = 1000~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**Step 1.** *Start from the SFEE. Which terms vanish for an insulated nozzle?*

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Insulated: $\dot{Q} \approx 0$; no work, $\dot{W} = 0$; $\Delta z \approx 0$. Left with (I): $(h_e - h_i) + \tfrac12(C_e^2 - C_i^2) = 0$."}
Insulated, so $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$; no work, $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$; and
$z_e \approx z_i$:
$$
0 = \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right)\right] \tag{I}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *For an ideal gas, how is the change in enthalpy related to the
change in temperature?*

::: {.gap height="10mm" hint="Ideal gas: $h_e - h_i = c_p(T_e - T_i)$ (II)."}
$$
h_e - h_i = c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right) \tag{II}
$$
:::

**Step 3.** *Combine (I) and (II): only $T_e$ is unknown.*

::: {.gap height="22mm" hint="$c_p(T_e - T_i) = -\tfrac12(C_e^2 - C_i^2)$, so $T_e = 200 - (600^2 - 10^2)/2000 = 20.05$ K."}
$$
c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
T_e = T_i - \frac{C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}}{2 c_p}
    = 200 - \frac{600^{2} - 10^{2}}{2 \times 1000}
    = \boxed{20.05~\mathrm{K}}
$$
The kinetic energy gained by the gas comes from its enthalpy, so the gas cools
down a lot.
:::
:::

### Turbines, pumps and compressors

A **turbine** is a device in which work is developed as a result of a gas or
liquid passing through a set of blades attached to a shaft.

![A gas or steam turbine (left) and a hydraulic turbine (right).](figures/img/ch4-turbines.png){width=80%}

**Compressors** are devices in which work is done on a **gas** passing
through them in order to raise the pressure. In **pumps**, the work input is
used to give energy to a **liquid** passing through.

![A reciprocating compressor, an axial compressor and a centrifugal pump.](figures/img/ch4-compressors-pumps.png){width=88%}

::: {.note}
A turbine delivers work, so $\dot{W}_\text{turbine} < 0$. Pumps and compressors
receive work, so $\dot{W}_\text{pump},\ \dot{W}_\text{compressor} > 0$.
:::

SFEE equation:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
$$

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Turbines, pumps, compressors: $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$, $\Delta KE \approx 0$, $\Delta PE \approx 0$."}
In turbines, pumps and compressors the heat transfer is usually small,
$\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$, and so are the changes of kinetic and potential
energy, $\tfrac{1}{2}(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}) \approx 0$ and
$g(z_e - z_i) \approx 0$.
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\text{Turbines, pumps and compressors:}\qquad
\dot{W}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$
:::

::: {.example}
The mass flow rate into a gas turbine is 1 kg/s. Determine the power output of
the turbine if the gas temperature drops 200 K during this process. (Assume
ideal gas and $c_p = 1000~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**Step 1.** *Which form does the SFEE take for a turbine?*

::: {.gap height="10mm" hint="Turbine: $\dot{W}_{cv} = \dot{m}(h_e - h_i)$."}
$$
\dot{W}_{cv} = \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Ideal gas: replace $\Delta h$ by $c_p \Delta T$. The temperature
drops, so what is the sign of $\Delta T$?*

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="$\Delta h = c_p\Delta T$ with $\Delta T = -200$ K: $\dot{W}_{cv} = 1 \times 1000 \times (-200) = -2\times10^5$ W."}
For an ideal gas $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$, with $\Delta T = -200$ K:
$$
\dot{W}_{cv} = 1~\mathrm{kg/s} \times 10^{3}~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times (-200~\mathrm{K})
= \boxed{-2\times10^{5}~\mathrm{J/s} = -200~\mathrm{kW}}
$$
$\dot{W}_{cv} < 0$: the turbine delivers 200 kW of power to the surroundings.
:::
:::

### Heat exchangers

Devices that transfer energy between fluids at different temperatures by heat
transfer are called **heat exchangers**.

![A boiler (left): the water in the tubes (green dashed control volume) receives heat, $\dot{Q} > 0$. A condenser (right): the steam gives heat to the cooling water, $\dot{Q} < 0$.](figures/img/ch4-heat-exchangers.png){width=90%}

SFEE equation:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
$$

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Heat exchangers: no shaft, $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$; $\Delta KE \approx 0$; $\Delta PE \approx 0$."}
A heat exchanger has no shaft or moving boundary, $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$, and the
changes of kinetic and potential energy are small,
$\tfrac{1}{2}(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}) \approx 0$ and $g(z_e - z_i) \approx 0$.
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\text{Heat exchangers:}\qquad
\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right),
\qquad
\dot{Q} > 0 \text{ boilers}, \quad \dot{Q} < 0 \text{ condensers}
$$
:::

## End-of-chapter problems {#sec-ch4-problems}

::: {.tryfirst}
Have a real go at every problem here before you look at a solution. Worked
solutions are released after the lectures, but reading a solution is not the
same as being able to produce one: the time you spend stuck on a problem is
where most of the learning happens. Only once you have an answer of your own,
or have tried every approach you can think of, check it against the solution,
and compare the method, not just the final number.
:::

**P4.1 [easy].** Air at 20 m/s, 1500 K, 875 kPa with 5 kg/s flows into a
turbine and it flows out at 25 m/s, 850 K, 105 kPa. Find the power output in
MW. (Assume air as an ideal gas with $c_p = 1005~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** $-3.27$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 3.27 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 2.68
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** $-2.68$

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
According to the SFEE, with $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$ and the kinetic and
potential energy changes $\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{W}_{cv} = \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$

For an ideal gas $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$, so
$$
\dot{W}_{cv} = \dot{m}\,c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right)
= 5~\mathrm{kg/s} \times 1005~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times (850 - 1500)~\mathrm{K}
= -3.27\times10^{6}~\mathrm{J/s}
= \boxed{-3.27~\mathrm{MW}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

Note $\dot{W} < 0$ for a turbine. The kinetic-energy term we neglected is only
$5 \times \tfrac{1}{2}\left(25^{2} - 20^{2}\right) \approx 0.56$ kW, tiny
compared with 3.27 MW.
:::
:::

**P4.2 [easy].** In a steam turbine the flow rate is 5000 kg/hour and the power
output is 500 kW. The heat loss from the turbine casing to the surroundings is
negligible (i.e. adiabatic process). Find the change in specific enthalpy of
the steam as it passes through the turbine, assuming that the mechanical
(kinetic and potential) energy of the steam is the same where it enters and
exits the turbine.

**(a)** 360 kJ/kg &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** $-100$ J/kg &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 100 J/kg
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** $-360$ kJ/kg

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
SFEE, with $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$ and the kinetic and potential energy
changes $\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{W}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
h_e - h_i \approx \frac{\dot{W}_{cv}}{\dot{m}}
$$

The power is an *output*, so $\dot{W}_{cv} = -500$ kW:
$$
h_e - h_i = \frac{-500\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J/s}}
{5000~\mathrm{kg/h} \times \dfrac{1~\mathrm{h}}{3600~\mathrm{s}}}
= -360\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J/kg}
= \boxed{-360~\mathrm{kJ/kg}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
:::
:::

**P4.3 [medium].** Air at 35 °C, 105 kPa flows in a
$100~\mathrm{mm} \times 150~\mathrm{mm}$ rectangular duct in a heating system.
The mass flow rate is 0.015 kg/s. What is the velocity of the air flowing in
the duct in m/s? (Assume air as an ideal gas with
$R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

![](figures/img/ch4-p-furnace.png){width=20%}

**(a)** 0.84 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 0.36 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 1.2 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 3.34

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
The cross-sectional area of the duct is
$$
A = 0.1~\mathrm{m} \times 0.15~\mathrm{m} = 0.015~\mathrm{m^2}
$$

Ideal gas, so
$$
\rho = \frac{P}{RT}
= \frac{105\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}}{287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times (273 + 35)~\mathrm{K}}
\approx 1.19~\mathrm{kg/m^3}
$$

Assuming a uniform velocity across the duct area, the mass flow rate is
$$
\dot{m} = \rho A C
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
C = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho A}
= \frac{0.015~\mathrm{kg/s}}{1.19~\mathrm{kg/m^3} \times 0.015~\mathrm{m^2}}
= \boxed{0.84~\mathrm{m/s}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P4.4 [medium].** A household fan of diameter 0.75 m takes air in at 98 kPa,
22 °C and delivers it at 105 kPa, 23 °C with a velocity of 1.5 m/s. What is the
inlet velocity in m/s? (Assume air as an ideal gas.)

![](figures/img/ch4-p-fan.png){width=20%}

**(a)** 3.7 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 2 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 1.6 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 1.3

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
If we assume steady-state conditions, with the inlet $i$ and exit $e$ as
sketched:

![](figures/img/ch4-p-fan-sol.png){width=24%}
$$
\dot{m}_i = \dot{m}_e
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\rho_i C_i A_i = \rho_e C_e A_e
$$

With $A_e = A_i$, and $\rho = P/(RT)$ from the ideal-gas assumption ($R$
cancels):
$$
\frac{C_i}{C_e} = \frac{\rho_e}{\rho_i}
= \frac{P_e/(R T_e)}{P_i/(R T_i)}
= \frac{P_e}{P_i}\,\frac{T_i}{T_e}
= \frac{105~\mathrm{kPa}}{98~\mathrm{kPa}} \times \frac{(273 + 22)~\mathrm{K}}{(273 + 23)~\mathrm{K}}
= 1.068
$$
$$
C_i = C_e \times 1.068 = 1.5~\mathrm{m/s} \times 1.068
= \boxed{1.6~\mathrm{m/s}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$
:::
:::

**P4.5 [medium].** In a jet engine a flow of air at 1000 K, 200 kPa and 40 m/s
enters a nozzle, where the air exits at 500 m/s, 90 kPa. What is the exit
temperature in kelvin, assuming no heat loss? (Assume air as an ideal gas with
$c_p = 1005~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 534 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 1510 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 876 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 123

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
The nozzle, with its inlet $i$ and exit $e$:

![](figures/img/ch4-p-nozzle-sol.png){width=36%}

According to the SFEE, with $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$, $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$ and
$z_e \approx z_i$:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\left(h_e - h_i\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) \approx 0
$$

For an ideal gas, $h_e - h_i = c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right)$:
$$
1005\left(T_e - 1000\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\left(500^{2} - 40^{2}\right) \approx 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\boxed{T_e \approx 876~\mathrm{K}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$

The pressures are not needed.
:::
:::

**P4.6 [medium].** A compressor brings nitrogen from 100 kPa, 290 K to
2000 kPa. The process has a work (per unit mass) input of 450 kJ/kg and the
exit temperature is 700 K. Find the heat transfer per unit mass in kJ/kg.
(Assume nitrogen as an ideal gas with $c_p = 1.04~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 36.9 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** $-23.6$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 524.3
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** $-191.8$

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
*Note: we are asked to find the heat transfer, so we should not neglect
$\dot{Q}$ in the SFEE.* With the kinetic and potential energy changes
$\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$

Dividing by $\dot{m}$:
$$
q_{cv} + w_{cv} \approx h_e - h_i
$$

For an ideal gas, $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$:
$$
q_{cv} + w_{cv} \approx c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
q_{cv} + 450~\mathrm{kJ/kg}
\approx 1.04~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)} \times (700 - 290)~\mathrm{K}
$$
$$
\boxed{q_{cv} = -23.6~\mathrm{kJ/kg}} \quad \text{(b)}
$$

**Note 1:** $q < 0$, meaning the compressor is losing energy through heat.

**Note 2:** as you can see, $|q| \ll |w|$. That is why we often neglect heat
transfer for turbines, compressors and pumps.
:::
:::

**P4.7 [medium].** Water enters a boiler at a rate of 1 kg/s with pressure
$P_1 = 1.013$ bar (standard atmospheric pressure) and $T_1 = 100$ °C. There is a
steady rate of heat input which causes the water to change to steam, which
leaves the tube at $P_2 = 1.013$ bar (unchanged) and $T_2 = 100$ °C (also
unchanged). How much heat is required to create the steam?

Assume that kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible. The standard
properties of water and steam at standard atmospheric pressure (1.013 bar) and
100 °C are:

| Property | Water | Steam | Units |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| $v$ | 0.001044 | 1.673 | $\mathrm{m^3/kg}$ |
| $u$ | 419.0 | 2506.5 | kJ/kg |
| $h = u + Pv$ | 419.1 | 2676.0 | kJ/kg |

**(a)** 2257 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 2426 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 2088 kW
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 2.3 W

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Take the tube as the control volume: water enters at $i$, steam leaves at $e$.

![](figures/img/ch4-p-boiler-sol.png){width=48%}

SFEE for the tube, with $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$ and the kinetic and potential energy
changes $\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} + \dot{W}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$

*Note: we cannot use $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$, since we do not have an ideal
gas.* (Indeed, here $\Delta T = 0$ but $\Delta h$ is large.) From the table:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 1~\mathrm{kg/s} \times
\left(2676~\mathrm{kJ/kg} - 419.1~\mathrm{kJ/kg}\right)
\approx \boxed{2257~\mathrm{kW}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

**Note:** $\dot{Q} > 0$ for boilers and $\dot{Q} < 0$ for condensers.

Using $u$ instead of $h$ gives $2506.5 - 419.0 = 2088$ kW, answer (c), which is
wrong: the SFEE contains the enthalpy, because it includes the flow work.
:::
:::

**P4.8 [hard].** In a factory, a compressor receives 600 kW power to compress
the air with a mass flow rate of 2 kg/s and temperature of 17 °C. The air
exiting from the compressor is then cooled by a cooler to 300 K. Find the heat
transfer in the cooler in kW. (Assume air as an ideal gas with
$c_p = 1.05~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.)

![](figures/img/ch4-p-compressor-cooler.png){width=66%}

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**SFEE for the compressor**, with $\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx 0$ and the kinetic and
potential energy changes $\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{W}_{cv} + \dot{Q}_{cv}
= \dot{m}\left[\left(h_e - h_i\right)
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(C_e^{2} - C_i^{2}\right) + g\left(z_e - z_i\right)\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{W}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
$$

With $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$ (ideal gas):
$$
600~\mathrm{kJ/s} = 2~\mathrm{kg/s} \times 1.05~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}
\times \left(T_e - (273 + 17)\right)~\mathrm{K}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
T_e = 575.7~\mathrm{K}
$$
This is the air temperature at the exit of the compressor.

**SFEE for the cooler**, with $\dot{W}_{cv} = 0$ and the kinetic and potential
energy changes $\approx 0$:
$$
\dot{Q}_{cv} \approx \dot{m}\left(h_e - h_i\right)
\quad\xrightarrow{\ \Delta h = c_p \Delta T\ }\quad
\dot{Q}_\text{cooler} \approx \dot{m}\,c_p\left(T_e - T_i\right)
$$

*Note:* the air leaves the compressor and enters the cooler, so
$T_{e,\text{comp}} = T_{i,\text{cooler}} = 575.7$ K:
$$
\dot{Q}_\text{cooler} \approx 2~\mathrm{kg/s} \times 1.05~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}
\times (300 - 575.7)~\mathrm{K}
\approx \boxed{-579~\mathrm{kW}}
$$

$\dot{Q} < 0$: 579 kW of heat is removed from the air in the cooler.
:::
:::
